title: Game style and inspiration collection website
author: curiousjbird
selftext:
Over the last 3 weeks, I've built (and launched on Google Play) 19 mobile games with Claude Code (a challenge I set for myself). During this process, one of the biggest obstacles was getting the game's "style" right. What I found, though, it wasn't Claude's fault—it was mine for not having the right words or a clear idea of the art direction. I usually approach a game from the mechanics or structure, and I start riffing on it with Claude using a default look, but then it gets ingrained in the game and becomes hard to change.

To help with this, and use up some spare tokens, I created an app/website: [styledex.games](http://styledex.games). 

![img](4yqqyvn8gnzh1 "Styledex.games screenshot")

It indexes over 1,500 games (and growing) from Steam, Google Play, iOS, and others. It tags their art styles, and links to their profiles (it doesn't store any assets). To start, you can search and save; if it gets some use, I want to add an api and an mcp server. It also includes prompt copy for each style you can use in your own project.

I'd appreciate any feedback!

Here are the categories I had Claude tag games with:

* **Rendering technique** (13 tags): how the image is made. Realistic 3D, stylized 3D, hand-drawn 2D, pixel art 
* **Named look** (25): recognizable overall aesthetics. Cozy diorama, gothic grimdark 3D, toybox, mobile casual gloss 
* **Shading model** (10): how surfaces are shaded. Soft gradient, physically based, flat/unshaded, cel shading 
* **Line work** (10): outlines and drawn lines. No outlines, thin clean outlines, thick outlines, bold ink 
* **Texture and surface** (20): surface marks and post effects. Clean, grime and wear, depth of field, glossy/wet 
* **Palette** (20): overall color strategy. Saturated, dark/low-key, earthy, desaturated 
* **Lighting** (18): light sources and atmosphere. Soft ambient, heavy bloom, colored light, fog/haze 
* **Character proportions** (10): Realistic, cute rounded, heroic stylized, chibi 
* **Detail density** (4): Minimalist, balanced, detailed, maximalist 
* **Dimension** (3): 2D, 3D, 2.5D 
* **Camera and perspective** (11): Third-person, first-person, top-down, side view, isometric 
* **Art influence** (37): art movements and media. Anime, gothic, Western comics, Western animation 
* **Era influence** (17): hardware generations and decades. 16-bit, 90s PC, early-2000s 3D, PS2 era 
* **Cultural influence** (19): Americana, European medieval, Japanese, Chinese 
* **Setting and theme** (18): Modern day, fantasy, sci-fi, horror 
* **Environment** (30): Forest, city, village, ocean and coast 
* **Mood and tone** (28): Tense, cheerful, chaotic, epic 
* **Game type** (18): Action, adventure, simulation, RPG 
* **Platform** (10): PC, Mac, mobile, Steam Deck, Switch, web



**tldr**: I created a website to tag games based on style and other attributes to help with game design inspiration

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
>I'd appreciate any feedback!

My feedback is stop shipping literal slop to the public that you've spent hardly any time building. 19 games in 3 weeks tells me you basically one-shotted them all and said "good enough". You're only making the anti-AI problem worse. Taints the rest of us AI devs that actually put time and effort into our stuff.

replies.author: curiousjbird
replies.body: Fair, but what I did was keep the games contained and focused; I created a "joy" manifesto for each game. I'm not trying to build epic RPGs, but cozy, small games. Games to relax with. One of them was a solitaire game--some of the biggest criticism from online research was how a lot of the current solitaire apps have too many ads, etc. So I created one with a simple bottom banner ad that you could remove with a one-time purchase (which helped me learn RevenueCat integration). Was amazed on Monday when I actually sold one. This was to help make my larger game ideas better--learn where the pitfalls of AI game development are, how to automate a lot of the backend stuff (Google Play, AdMob, Sentry, RevenueCat, Firebase, OpenRouter for art assets, etc), and how to rapidly test and iterate. Most of my games had 50+ iterations--I built a pipeline of having 3-5 games in development at various stages. I'd sit down, open Google Recorder on my phone and start a test session. I'd just narrate the gameplay and any issues. I'd upload it to the Claude session, then work on the next one. It was pretty exhausting; my original goal was 30, but I got a bit burnt out. Now I have about 5-6 deeply personal games that I'm working on--these will have more depth and refinement.

replies.author: dank_summers
replies.body: Agreed, you should spend at least few weeks fleshing out a single idea to determine if it's worthwhile. 1 published game a day sounds insane

replies.author: curiousjbird
replies.body: I've got a list of 50+ game ideas (keeps growing). My workflow is to have several in various stages of brainstorming with Claude (using desktop app), researching a particular genre, etc. From that pool I'd fire up a Claude Code (CLI) session based on my "gamekit" (set of tools I have settled on), have it lay out the game foundation and then create a playable prototype of the main joy moment of the game. I'll have a couple of other games further along and then one game that was "done" (I have a polish skill I used) and was getting all of the plumbing set up for admob and other tools and then getting published. So the lifecycle of any particular game is 1-3 weeks. I tried to so something different for each game, 3d vs 2d. Sound. Multi-player. Art style. After I publish I let it sit for a couple of days and then go back to it to see what I missed, if I still found it fun. Some of my more recent ones have more depth so need longer to gestate. My favorite is a game based on a paperroute I had as a kid in the 80s. I built in real headlines by scrapping newspapers from that era and location. I'm trying to be careful about slop. My 20 something kids keep me in check. But without a deadline and a goal of  publishing I just was meandering around.

comments.author: curiousjbird
comments.body: \~$0.50 in AdMob revenue and $4 in a one-time purchase. Not nothing. I haven't promoted them yet, that is the next phase of my master plan.
